newsitem.title: FRANCE: Human body parts may be latest Paris couture craze.
newsitem.headline: Human body parts may be latest Paris couture craze.

text.p: The Autumn-Winter haute couture season opened in Paris on Sunday amid a furore over a report that Monday's Givenchy collection by British designer Alexander McQueen will contain human body parts.
McQueen, who was hired by Givenchy in October, is recycling bits of human bone, teeth and other body parts in the house's couture collection, according to The Sunday Times of London.
Givenchy spokesman Eric Lanuit denied the police had received a complaint about the new collection, but refused to comment when asked whether the clothes included human bones, whether real or fake.
Instead, he urged a reporter to see the Givenchy show when it is unveiled on Monday, ironically, at a Paris medical school.
McQueen, a 28-year-old fashion subversive whose father was a taxi driver, has previously used human hair, blood, insects and reptile skulls in London catwalk shows for his signature label.

Meanwhile, Italian designer Gianni Versace, in a collection he characterised as "a kind of Byzantine minimalism" and "neo-Japanese", unveiled a show consisting largely of tight black dresses with heavily padded, angular shoulders.

Asymmetry was a contant thread, with thick shoulder pads protruding from the slashed-off sleeve of a mini-dress or tucked into the spaghetti strap of leather evening gowns embroidered with Byzantine crosses or Japanese symbols.
But there was a disturbing aggressiveness in the knife sharp angle of a shoulder, the menacing stiletto heels and the blackened eyes of the models.
Earlier, in the first shows of the season, French fashion houses Nina Ricci and Torrente showed collections aiming for mature women who shun the less-is-more fashion ideal.
Gerard Pipart focused on striking hues at Nina Ricci -- mallard green, peacock blue, shocking pink -- for a show brimming with animal paraphernalia.

Anaconda and python skin jackets, peacock and ostrich feather headdresses, mink, fox or sable edging on velvet evening jackets and satin tunics -- the show erased any last trace of faith in Paris' commitment to environment-friendly fashion.
The event was nonetheless marked by a protest.
Seamstresses from Nina Ricci's couture atelier demonstrated outside the house's Avenue de Montaigne headquarters against a cost-cutting plan to lay-off 35 of the house's 67 employees.
"There is no desire here to seek out clients for haute couture," said Brigitte Memery, a delegate from the CGT labour union and a seamstress at Nina Ricci for the past 24 years.

Memery said the house currently counts only about 10 couture customers, lending weight to unofficial reports that only a few hundred clients can still afford to pay the astronomical sums needed to buy a one-of-a-kind couture gown. The house makes most of its money from perfumes and accessories.
The Chambre Syndicale, French fashion's governing body, ever determined to portray couture as a thriving industry, maintains there are still 2,000 women wealthy enough to buy the costly creations.

At Torrente, designer Rosette Mett recycled the dandy look, matching tweed riding coats with ascots and waistcoats over white poplin shirts, then threw political correctness to the wind by trimming wool coats with voluminous cuffs and collars of fox fur, mink or ostrich feathers.
Satin, in splashy shocking pink and chartreuse or icy blue, pearl and silver, was the fabric of choice for evening sheaths or dinner jackets, with sequins flashing at pockets and lapels.

Fashion houses often call on famous faces to appear on their catwalks to boost their visibility, and Torrente was no exception. Charlie Chaplin's grandaughter Dolores was the bride in spreading skirts and mink-edged jacket of ivory faille silk.
